analysis.one_liner: Requires federal licenses and registration for all firearms and ammunition, and bans large-capacity magazines.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Judiciary Committee, drew zero cosponsors, and received no vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required everyone in the United States to obtain a federal license to possess a firearm or ammunition and to register every gun with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. To get a license, a person would need to pass a background check, complete a government-approved psychological evaluation, finish at least 24 hours of certified training, and pay $800 for a liability insurance policy issued by the Justice Department. It would also have banned ammunition of .50 caliber or larger and magazines holding more than 10 rounds, with prison terms of up to 25 years for violations.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, people exposed to gun violence would be the intended beneficiaries: every buyer would undergo a background check, a psychological evaluation, and safety training, and all guns would be registered in a database available to law enforcement. The ban on .50-caliber ammunition and large-capacity magazines would remove the highest-volume weapons from civilian circulation. Law enforcement would gain a registry of every gun and its owner.

how_it_helps.text: Would require anyone possessing a firearm or ammunition to hold a federal license issued only after a criminal background check, a psychological evaluation, and completion of at least 24 hours of certified safety training.

Would require every firearm in the United States to be registered with ATF, with the owner's identity, where the gun is stored, and who it is loaned to, all logged in a national database available to law enforcement at every level.
Would prohibit possession of ammunition .50 caliber or greater and any magazine or feeding device holding more than 10 rounds, with exceptions only for government and law-enforcement uses.
Would require every licensed gun owner to carry a liability insurance policy issued by the Attorney General, purchased for an $800 fee, covering losses and damages from use of the firearm.

analysis.who_pays: Gun owners would pay directly: an $800 annual insurance fee to the Justice Department, licensing and training costs, and the time burden of psychological evaluations that could include interviews of spouses, former spouses, and associates. Knowing possession of an unlicensed, unregistered gun would carry a mandatory fine of at least $75,000 and 15 to 25 years in prison, so even otherwise-lawful owners who missed a deadline would face felony exposure. The firearms industry would lose sales from the magazine and ammunition bans and the extra license required for military-style weapons.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun owners and the firearms industry

drawbacks.text: Penalties are extreme relative to the conduct: knowingly possessing a firearm or ammunition without a license would carry a fine of at least $75,000 and 15 to 25 years in prison, and transferring a gun to someone under 18 could bring 25 to 40 years — terms that would fall hardest on ordinary owners who miss a registration or renewal deadline.
The registry database would be open to all members of the public, not just law enforcement, publishing the identity, address, and storage location of every gun owner in the country.

The $800 annual insurance fee and the required psychological evaluations — which could extend to interviews with spouses, ex-spouses, and other household members — are costly and burdensome, and the fee weighs most heavily on lower-income owners.

License denial is mandatory for anyone ever hospitalized with a mental illness or diagnosis including depression, dementia, or Alzheimer's, a broad lifetime disqualification that could deter people from seeking mental health care.
The bill had no realistic path: not a single member of either party cosponsored it, and it sat in committee for the rest of the Congress.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated goal — fewer shootings through universal background checks, training, registration, and a ban on large magazines — addresses a real public-safety problem. But the design goes far beyond most gun-regulation proposals: it criminalizes unlicensed possession with 15-to-25-year minimum terms, publishes the entire registry to the public, charges $800 a year, and requires psychological evaluations that reach into applicants' marriages and households. The costs would fall on millions of ordinary gun owners, and the bill's zero cosponsors — including among Democrats who controlled the House — signals that even sympathetic lawmakers judged the burden and penalty structure too heavy for the safety benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then a crime subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended — no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee introduced the bill on July 26, 2019, naming it for Sabika Sheikh.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day, and on August 28, 2019 to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security.
No further action was ever taken: no markup, no hearing, no floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The bill never attracted a single cosponsor in the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun owners keep the current rules, and firearms makers and dealers keep selling under existing law. Supporters of tighter gun regulation gained nothing; no licensing, registration, or magazine ban was enacted.

against.what_they_did: No member of either party cosponsored the bill, leaving it without any support to advance it.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no member of either party signed on, so no partisan split was ever measured — the bill was a single-sponsor measure with zero cosponsors.

industries.note: Universal licensing and registration, an extra license for military-style weapons, and bans on magazines over 10 rounds and .50-caliber ammunition would shrink what the industry could sell. Its interest in unrestricted sales ran against the bill's public-safety aim.
The bill mandates at least 24 hours of Attorney General-certified training for every applicant, plus recurring renewal courses, creating a captive customer base for certified instructors.

Every license applicant would need a psychological evaluation conducted by an approved psychologist, with follow-up interviews of family and associates, generating paid evaluations for the profession. The mandate serves the bill's safety screening but adds cost for applicants.
